crosscheck_source: Pearson GSE Grammar for adult learners 2023
crosscheck_policy: GSE Grammar is supporting/cross-check evidence mapped to reviewed grammar supercategories; it does not create a second independent target inventory.
grammar_family_stage_policy: Only lifecycle stages explicitly present in the reviewed grammar-family source are copied; missing early-level stages are not invented.

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use a range of modals with passive infinitives referring to the present or future.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: It could be done. It could be improved. The train might be delayed.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Modal verb | Likelihood Modal verb | Ability Verb | Passive

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can refer to certainty and probability using ‘certain/likely/due to’ with verb phrases.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: He’s certain to pass the exam. The train is likely to be late. When are they due to arrive?
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Phrase | With ‘be’ Phrase | With infinitive

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can omit the relative pronoun in defining (restrictive) relative clauses.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.structure: omission of relative pronoun in defining/ restrictive clause
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: He’s the friend (who) I told you about. That’s the movie (that) I wanted to see.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Clause | Relative

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use ‘need’ with the passive infinitive to express necessity.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: The report needs to be completed this week. Homework needs to be handed in today.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Modal verb | Obligation Phrase | With infinitive Verb | Passive

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can express alternative conditions with ‘whether … or not’.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: Whether she likes it or not, she’s coming with us. The show starts tomorrow, whether or not it rains.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Conjunction | Coordinating Clause | Conditional

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can describe beliefs and opinions using verbs of judgement and evaluation in the passive.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: It’s believed that he died in Iraq. It’s expected that students will graduate in three years.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Verb | Passive Clause | Dependent Clause | Reported speech and ideas

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use clauses with ‘It’ + ‘be’ … to emphasise the topic or main point.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: It’s the money that keeps me in this job. It was his accent that made him hard to understand.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Clause | Clefting and fronting Phrase | With ‘be’

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use verb phrases with ‘to’ + infinitive as subject and complement.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: My dream is to live in New York. The effect of the drug was to give him a headache.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Phrase | With infinitive

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use clauses with ‘What ...’ to emphasise the topic or main point.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: What we need now is a good night’s sleep. What I said was that I don’t need your help.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Clause | Clefting and fronting Clause | Relative

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can soften orders and requests by using verbs like ‘thought’, ‘wondered’, etc. in the past tense.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.structure: softening orders and requests with past tense
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: I thought perhaps you could help me. We hoped you’d come to our party. I was wondering if you could get me a ticket for the concert?
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Verb | Tense

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use ‘while’, ‘whereas’ and ‘whilst’ (Br Eng) to contrast and compare actions and situations.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: You enjoy running, whereas I find it very boring. While(st) I sympathise with you, I can’t forget about what you did.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Conjunction | Concession and contrast Clause | Comparison

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can talk about past plans and intentions using ‘(not) meant/supposed to’ + infinitive.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: It was meant to be fun. He wasn’t supposed to do that.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Verb | Passive Phrase | With infinitive

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can express prohibition in the present or future with ‘forbid’ and ‘(not) allow’.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: I forbid you to speak to him. We won’t be allowed to take pictures.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Phrase | With infinitive Verb | Passive

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can report orders, requests and advice with infinitive clauses.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: She told me not to do it. He warned us not to be late. She encouraged him to study.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Phrase | With infinitive Clause | Reported speech and ideas

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can express negative purpose with ‘so as/ in order not to’.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.structure: so as/in order’ + ‘not to’ + VPinf for negative purpose
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: In order not to seem stupid, he didn’t say anything. I came in very quietly, so as not to wake anyone.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Conjunction | Cause and result Phrase | With infinitive Clause | Negation

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can correctly use defining (restrictive) and non-defining (non- restrictive) relative clauses.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.structure: defining (restrictive) vs. non-defining (non- restrictive) relative clauses
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: I told my sister, who already knew what happened. Tell only the people who need the information.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Clause | Relative

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use the future continuous with reference to actions in progress at a specific time in the future.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: This time tomorrow I’ll be flying to Rio. I’ll be driving home from work at 5 p.m. this evening.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Verb | Tense Adverb | Time

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use adverbials such as ‘however’, ‘on the other hand’, and ‘though’ to express concession.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: I don’t earn much - however, I have plenty of free time. We’ll get there quicker by train. On the other hand, the bus is much cheaper.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Conjunction | Concession and contrast Clause | Dependent

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can make statements about appearance using ‘seem/appear’ (+ ‘like/that’) with complement clauses.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: It looks like he isn’t coming. It appears that John has misunderstood.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Clause | Dependent Clause | Reported speech and ideas

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can construct phrases with ‘(not) worth ...’ and ‘(no) point ...’ to express the (lack of) usefulness or value of an action or suggestion.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.structure: expressing (lack of) use or value in an action with ‘(not) worth/(no) point (in)’ + VPgerund
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: There’s no point in talking about it. It’s not worth repairing such an old car.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Phrase | With gerund (-ing)

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can emphasise a statement by adding ‘do’ or ‘did’.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.structure: additional auxiliary ‘do’ or ‘did’ for stress or emphasis
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: He does look nice in his new suit. I didn’t get to see John, but I did see his mother.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Verb | Auxiliary

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can express past intentions and plans with ‘thinking of’ and verbs in the gerund.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: We were thinking of selling the house. Were you thinking of driving there?
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Phrase | With gerund (-ing) Preposition | Complementiser Verb | Tense

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use non-defining (non-restrictive) relative clauses to make a comment.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: He was late, which was unusual. It’s raining, which is really annoying.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Clause | Relative

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can describe past beliefs and opinions using ‘it was’ + passive forms of verbs of judgement and evaluation.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.structure: it’s/it was thought/believed/considered/ etc.(that)’ + complement clause
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: It was expected that women would get married in their 20s. It was thought that all the records had been destroyed.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Verb | Passive Clause | Dependent Verb | Tense

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can speak about information acquired from others using ‘hear’ + ‘(that +)’ complement clause.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: I hear that John and Susie are getting married. I’ve heard that Martin’s lost his job.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Clause | Reported speech and ideas Conjunction | Coordinating

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use ‘ought(n’t) to’ to offer or ask for advice or suggestions.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: You ought to go to a doctor. He oughtn’t to drink so much. Where ought we to go?
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Modal verb | Obligation Phrase | With infinitive

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use ‘as soon as’ with the past simple and past perfect.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.structure: ‘as soon as’ + past simple + past perfect
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: I handed the work in as soon as I had finished it. As soon as she’d eaten, she fell asleep.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Conjunction | Time Verb | Tense

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use the past perfect continuous in a range of common situations.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: I’d been living in London for three years when I met her. How long had you been waiting when I arrived?
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Verb | Tense Verb | Auxiliary

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use a range of common reporting verbs with ‘that’ + complement clause.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: He suggested that we come back later. She warned me that she would have to tell her father.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Clause | Reported speech and ideas Conjunction | Coordinating Clause | Dependent

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use ‘I wish/if only …’ to express regrets and wishes about the past.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: If only I’d worked harder. I wish we’d bought that house.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Modal verb | Wishes and intentions Verb | Tense

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can make complex comparisons between verb/noun phrases.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: Being happy is more important than making money. The loss of his job made a bigger difference than the end of his marriage.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Adjective | Comparison Conjunction | Coordinating

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use ‘need’ with verbs in the gerund to express necessity.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: My hair needs cutting. The children need picking up.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Modal verb | Obligation Phrase | With gerund (-ing)

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use the past perfect with adverbial clauses of time.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.structure: past perfect with adverbial clauses of time
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: I remembered it after I’d already left home. By the time I got there she’d gone.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Clause | Time Verb | Tense Adverb | Time

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use the past perfect passive.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: The goods had already been stolen. It had all been said before. The show had been cancelled.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Verb | Passive Verb | Tense

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use noun phrases in place of verb phrases in formal written language.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: The weather has changed, which surprised us. vs. The change in the weather surprised us. The money disappeared, which puzzled Marian. vs. Marian was puzzled by the disappearance of the money.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Clause | Basic construction hrase | Clefting and fronting

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use gerunds in the passive form as complement.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: My mother loves being taken out. Children enjoy being read to.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Phrase | With gerund (-ing) Verb | Passive

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use a range of complex conjunctions in conditional statements (all three types).
gse_crosscheck_evidence.structure: clause1 (action or event) + ‘on condition that/as long as/ providing that/provided that’ + clause 2 (condition)
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: on condition that as long as providing/provided that
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Clause | Conditional Conjunction | Cause and result

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use ‘will’ + infinitive for orders and instructions.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: You will do as you are told. They will wait till they’re called.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Modal verb | Obligation Verb | Imperative Verb | Tense

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can make complex comparisons between clauses.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: There’s more work to do than we have time for. She was more concerned with getting the job done than with doing it well.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Adjective | Comparison Conjunction | Coordinating

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can express purpose using ‘so as to’ with infinitive clauses.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: I got up at 6:00 so as to be on time. So as to keep fit, I go for a run every morning.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Conjunction | Cause and result Phrase | With infinitive

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can express regrets and preferences with ‘would rather/it’s time’ with past tense clauses.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: I’d rather we stayed in tonight. I’d rather we went to the cinema. It’s time we left.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Modal verb | Wishes and intentions

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use ‘as if/as though’ with the present simple to refer to what appears to be the case.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.structure: ‘as if/as though’ + complement clause (present; equivalent to first conditional)
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: It looks as though they’re not coming.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Clause | Conditional Verb | Tense

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can omit subject + ‘be’ after ‘if’ in fixed expressions.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: if necessary, if any, if anything, if in doubt
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Clause | Conditional Phrase | Basic construction

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use ‘shall’ + infinitive for formal first- person statements about the future.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: I shall do my best.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Modal verb | Wishes and intentions Verb | Tense

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use the future perfect with reference to actions to be completed by a specific time in the future.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: I’ll have finished it by Saturday. The match won’t have finished by 8 p.m.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Verb | Tense Adverb | Time Preposition | Time

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use adverbial phrases to make comments.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: Practically speaking … At the end of the day... Taking the long view…
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Adverb | Modifier Phrase | Clefting and fronting

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use the future perfect passive.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: The job will have been completed by next month. The package will have been delivered before you get home.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Verb | Passive Verb | Tense

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use ‘it is/was believed/reported that’ + VP to report beliefs, reportes, rumours, etc.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: It’s now believed that over 300 people died in the fire. It was reported that the army had taken control of the capital.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Clause | Reported speech and ideas

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can describe hypothetical current results of a past action or situation using ‘would …’ with the third conditional.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: If I’d worked harder at school, I’d have a better job now. She would be here now if anyone had told her about the party.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Clause | Conditional Clause | Result/cause Verb | Tense

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use initial ‘No matter’ with relative pronouns for emphatic statements about the present and near future.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: No matter what you say, I’m coming. No matter how much it costs, we’re buying it.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Clause | Clefting and fronting Clause | Relative

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can express beliefs and opinions with ‘is/ are/was/were’ + ‘thought/believed to…’.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: He’s thought to be about 50. Everyone was believed to have died in the fire.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Verb | Passive Phrase | With infinitive Clause | Reported speech and ideas

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use ‘should’ in hypothetical statements about the present and near future with inversion and omission of ‘if’.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: Should you wish to invest in the business, please contact our office.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Clause | Conditional Verb | Tags and question forms

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use ‘as if/as though’ with the past simple to refer to hypothetical or counterfactual circumstances.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.structure: ‘as if/as though’ + complement clause (past simple; equivalent to second conditional)
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: You talk as though we didn’t know each other.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Clause | Conditional Verb | Tense

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can ask questions with ‘is it/was it’ and complement clauses.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: What was it you wanted? Where is it that you were brought up?
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Phrase | Clefting and fronting Clause | Relative

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use a range of cleft sentences in the present, past and future.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: The fact is that we can’t go. What we’ll do is call the airport. What we did in the end was to apologise.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Phrase | Clefting and fronting

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can add information using ‘not only … but also …’
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: The information is not only poorly presented, but also inaccurate.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Clause | Result/cause

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can order a sequence of events using an appended clause with present participle or ‘having’ + past participle.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.structure: reduced adverbial clauses with present participle or ‘having’ + past participle
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: Walking into the room, I bumped into Hiro. Having bought the tickets, we went for a coffee.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Clause | Appended (participle) Clause | Dependent

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can describe present or future outcomes of a hypothetical situation using initial ‘only if’ with inversion of subject and object.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: Only if you pay now will you avoid prosecution. Only if the weather conditions became much worse would they turn back.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Clause | Conditional Clause | Clefting and fronting

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use ‘one’s’ as an impersonal possessive adjective.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: One should always do one’s best.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Pronoun | Generic/impersonal Noun | Possessive (genitive)

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use ‘on the point of’ (Br Eng) to talk about imminent events in the present and past.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.structure: immediate future with ‘on the point of’ + VPgerund
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: She’s on the point of leaving her job. We were on the point of going out when Jane called.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Adverb | Time Phrase | With gerund (-ing)

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use ‘as if/as though’ with the past perfect to refer to hypothetical (counterfactual) circumstances in the past.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.structure: ‘as if/as though’ + complement clause (past perfect; equivalent to third conditional)
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: The house looked as though no one had lived there for years.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Clause | Conditional Conjunction | Coordinating Verb | Tense

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can use ‘since …’ to talk about reasons, causes and explanations.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: Since you don’t need your car today, can I borrow it? I assumed that you were out, since the lights were off.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Clause | Result/cause Conjunction | Cause and result

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can express impersonal belief and opinion using ‘thought/believed to …’
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: Leonardo is often thought to be the greatest artist who ever lived. This is believed to be the most valuable diamond in the world.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Phrase | With infinitive Verb | Passive

gse_crosscheck_evidence.source_text: Can invert subject and verb after initial complex adverbials.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.example: In no way do I approve of the way he talked to you. Under no circumstances should you approach him.
gse_crosscheck_evidence.grammatical_categories: Clause | Clefting and fronting
